blocks.text: The sex of an animal is determined during its embryonic development. In most animals sex is determined on the basis of the karyotype, the appearance of the complete set of chromosomes in the cells, which includes their number, size and shape.

In the karyotype of most animals all pairs of chromosomes are alike in females and males except one. The chromosomes that are perfectly alike in both are autosomes; the one pair that differs and determines the sex are the sex chromosomes.

blocks.alt: Left: Drosophila, female with three pairs of autosomes (two large, one tiny) and two rod-shaped X chromosomes, male with the same autosomes plus one X and a hook-shaped Y. Right: a human set of 22 numbered autosome pairs getting smaller from 1 to 22, drawn as blue and red partners, and below them female XX and male XY, the Y much smaller.
blocks.caption: Autosomes and sex chromosomes in Drosophila and humans (original schematic after Figure 18.12).
blocks.long_description: A karyotype is the complete set of chromosomes of a cell, described by their number, size and shape. All pairs are alike in males and females except one: the alike ones are autosomes and the odd pair are the sex chromosomes. Drosophila has 3 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes; humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes. In both, females are XX and males XY, the Y being hook-shaped in Drosophila and much smaller than the X in humans. This schematic is not to scale.

blocks.prompt: How many autosomes does a human body cell have?
blocks.explanation: 44, in 22 pairs, plus one pair of sex chromosomes, 46 in all.

items: Karyotype: number, size and shape of a cell's chromosomes.
Autosomes alike in both sexes; one pair of sex chromosomes differs.
